1.pericope_label: If there be any consolation in Christ, fulfil ye my joy
debates: What the first word of the appeal means: Gill entertains both consolation and exhortation, Clarke reports that several critics prefer exhortation, Calvin sets that reading out and then rejects it as answering the context less well, while Ellicott makes it encouragement, the stirring up of spiritual activity, and Robertson renders it a ground of appeal

Whether unity of judgment or of affection comes first: Henry holds that Christians should be one in affection whether they can be one in apprehension or not, affection being always in their power and the likeliest way to bring them nearer in judgment, while Calvin puts harmony of views first and calls it the beginning of love, though not sufficient without joined hearts; Barnes wishes perfect unity of sentiment and plan were attainable but settles for what will prevent discord

Whether the apostle appeals as a father: Chrysostom frames the whole verse as a father claiming a return for the care of nourishing his son, while Calvin notes that Paul deliberately humbles himself and implores their pity where he might have used his paternal authority and demanded respect from them as his sons
outliers: Robertson's report of the conjecture that the disagreement of gender and number in the fourth clause is an error of an early transcriber, or even of the man who took the letter down from dictation

Barnes's judgment that there is probably no single thing so much insisted on in the New Testament as harmony among Christians, and almost nothing so little known, and that if it prevailed the world would soon be converted to God
Chrysostom's saying that there is nothing better and nothing more affectionate than a spiritual teacher, who surpasses the kindness of any natural father
Calvin's reason for the urgency, that disagreement invariably opens a door for Satan to disseminate impious doctrines, agreement being the best bulwark for repelling them
Wesley's distribution of the three clauses among the three Persons, and Robertson's images of souls that beat together and clocks that strike at the same moment

3.pericope_label: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus
debates: Whether esteeming others better means judging them morally superior: Ellicott denies it outright, holding that what is ascribed is a higher place and dignity rather than moral superiority, while Clarke and Wesley ground the estimate in self-knowledge, since every man knows more evil of himself than he can know of another, and Robertson renders the participle neutrally as excelling

How far the command to look on the things of others reaches: Ellicott guards it against a denial of all self-love, a man being individual as well as social, Barnes guards it against intermeddling and unsought advice, and Gill guards it by insisting that a man must still provide for his own household, referring the command chiefly to spiritual gifts

Why the example of Christ is produced at this point: Chrysostom holds that nothing rouses a great soul to good works so much as learning that in them it is likened to God, Calvin divides the appeal into imitation as the rule of life and as the road to true glory, and Robertson makes it simply the one way to secure unity
outliers: Robertson's note that the word for lowliness of mind is late and rare, absent from the Old Testament and the early Greek writers and used in a bad sense for pusillanimity by Josephus and Epictetus, one of the words Christianity has ennobled and dignified

Barnes's catalogue of the ways the rule is broken, denominations attempting to outstrip each other, ministers preaching with no better aim, competition in dress and equipage, and benevolence itself pursued with the secret aim of outdoing others

Calvin's diagnosis of the two pests, contention which rushes headlong once it has entered and vainglory which is offended at seeing others superior, with ambition as the bellows that kindles all strifes and humility as the single remedy for both
Gill's qualification that all striving is not forbidden, since they were to strive for the faith of the gospel and the purity of its ordinances, worship and discipline

Chrysostom's list of the examples the Lord set before his disciples, himself, the Father and the prophets, with the apostle following the same method where he urges liberality by the poverty of Christ

6.pericope_label: Who, being in the form of God, made himself of no reputation
debates: What the form of God is: Clarke argues that whatever it was he divested himself of it, so that it can be neither the divine nature nor the government of the world nor the power of miracles, and concludes for the visible glory in which the Deity dwells, the word meaning external appearance and not essence; Calvin likewise makes it majesty, illustrated by the insignia of a king or a magistrate; against them Ellicott holds that the word describes the specific character which makes each being what it is, so that essential and eternal being in the true nature of God is asserted, and Robertson and Wesley agree, Wesley calling it the incommunicable nature — which sets him against Clarke, of his own school. Barnes sets out both possibilities without deciding

Of what he emptied himself: Gill, Barnes and Calvin all insist that nothing was lost and the glory was only covered, Barnes comparing the sun behind a cloud whose beams are not extinguished and Calvin calling the abasement of the flesh a veil, while Wesley says he not only veiled but in some sense renounced the glory he had before the world began, and Robertson allows real limitations of space, knowledge and power while denying any limitation by error

Whether the emptying belongs to the manhood only: Calvin raises the question, reports that Erasmus answered yes, objects that the form of God was there before he became man, and answers that the apostle speaks of Christ entire while the thing applies to one nature only, as when we call man mortal and mean his body
outliers: Calvin's figures for the form of God, that as a man is known by the look of his face so the majesty shining forth in God is his form, and better, that it is the sceptre and crown and mantle by which a king is known, or the purple-bordered robe and ivory seat of a magistrate
Barnes's figure of the sun obscured by a cloud or in an eclipse, whose glory is not really changed and whose beams are not extinguished, its lustre being only for a time hidden
Robertson's report of the phrase that he stripped himself of the insignia of majesty, with his warning that here above all men should show restraint and modesty
Ellicott's observation that the glory laid down at the incarnation was resumed for a moment at the transfiguration and worn anew at the ascension
Cyril of Jerusalem's use of the clause to comfort the poor and the enslaved before the judgment seat, that he who took the form of a servant does not despise servants
Wesley's distinction of the three terms, the form expressing something absolute, the likeness referring to other things of the same kind, and the fashion respecting what appears to sight and sense

8.pericope_label: He became obedient unto death; wherefore God also hath highly exalted him
debates: Whether the death is set forth here as an atonement: Ellicott denies it expressly, holding that in that light it could be no pattern to us, and reads it as the completion of the obedience of a whole life, while Clarke treats the same clause as atonement outright, Calvin adds that by dying so he was accursed in the sight of God, and Cyril of Jerusalem states the substitution most fully, that God must either destroy all men in his truth or cancel the sentence in his loving-kindness, and preserved both

What the name above every name is: Robertson takes it naturally for the name Jesus given in the next verse, while reporting the alternatives; Ellicott takes it for the Name of God, properly Jehovah, confirming this from the adoration that follows, which the prophet claims as the sole due of God; Wesley and Barnes keep to dignity and majesty above every creature; Clarke notes the article read by good authorities

Whether the verse warrants bowing at the mention of the name: Barnes denies it flatly and says the custom in some churches arose entirely from a misinterpretation, Gill presses that the name was common among the Jews so the bare sound commands no peculiar respect and that several creatures named have no knees, Robertson calls it no matter of perfunctory genuflection, while Ellicott takes the phrase as the standing expression for worship offered to God and Calvin insists on outward profession as well as inward affection

Who the beings under the earth are: Clarke takes them for those in the shades below who died without receiving salvation, or else fallen spirits, Gill names angels, departed souls and devils together, Robertson gives the word as the old adjective for the departed and simply the dead, and Wesley takes the three classes as the whole universe
outliers: Barnes's citation of a history of the Puritans in support of his claim that the custom of bowing at the name rests on this one passage and on a misreading of it
Gill's argument that Joshua bore the same name and a sorcerer was called Barjesus, so that it would be ridiculous to bow at the reading of those passages
Robertson's question what glory Christ had after the ascension that he had not before, and what he carried back to heaven that he did not bring, with his answer that it was his humanity
Calvin's protest against those who make the passage prove that Christ merited first for himself and afterwards for others, which he calls a suggestion of Satan
Clarke's five steps of the humiliation, including the observation that he was not naturally liable to death, having never sinned, and had a right in his human nature to immortality

Robertson's report of the lament that Lord has become one of the most lifeless words in the Christian vocabulary, when it really declares the character and dignity of Christ and is the basis and object of worship

12.pericope_label: Work out your own salvation, for it is God which worketh in you
debates: How much of the willing and doing is left to man: Clarke holds that God gives the power to will and to act while the use of those powers belongs to man, who is accountable for them, and that God neither wills for man nor works in his stead; Calvin ascribes both the inclination and the power to carry it into effect wholly to God and attacks the schoolmen who would give free will a separate power to co-operate with grace, Gill adding that the grace works efficaciously and not by moral persuasion; Barnes holds a middle line by negatives, that God neither acts for us nor compels us against our will; Ellicott calls it a paradox irreconcilable to our logic which Scripture leaves unreconciled; and Robertson says the apostle exhorts like an Arminian when addressing men and prays like a Calvinist when addressing God

How strong the fear and trembling is: Chrysostom takes the second word for an excessive degree of fear and asks who ever learnt even his letters without it, and Clarke and Henry refer it to the danger of miscarrying and coming short, while Robertson passes on two milder glosses, wholesome serious caution and a nervous anxiety to do right, and Ellicott relates it instead to the reverence of a servant toward a superior

What working out requires: Henry presses that the word means working thoroughly and taking true pains, not doing something now and then but persevering to the end, while Ellicott makes it the carrying to completion of what God has begun, man’s co-operation being secondary and intermediate
outliers: Robertson's aside that God is the Energy and the Energizer of the universe, with his approving report that physicists of his own day were not afraid to agree with the apostle and to put God behind gravitation and all the laws of nature
Chrysostom's rule that admonitions ought to be accompanied with commendations, so that those admonished are referred to the measure of zeal they have themselves already shown

Ellicott's analogy for the inner working, that we are familiar with the influence of one created will upon another, real though limited and in no sense compulsive, from which we may catch a faint glimpse of the working of the Spirit of God upon the spirit of man
Ellicott's observation that this is the only epistle which contains no direct rebuke
Gill's report that a royal manuscript adds a word making the operation more emphatic still, so that the grace is said to work in them by power
Wesley's exclamation at the encouragement, that the arm of Omnipotence is stretched out for our support and our succour

14.pericope_label: Do all things without murmurings, and shine as lights in the world
debates: Who the crooked and perverse generation are: Barnes thinks it not improbable that the Jews at Philippi were particularly meant, the phrase being taken from the song of Moses, and Clarke says the same, while Wesley applies it to the bulk of mankind, crooked by a corrupt nature and more perverse by custom and practice, and Calvin describes only believers intermingled with unbelievers on every side; Ellicott traces the wording to the same passage without narrowing its application

What holding forth the word means: Ellicott keeps the figure of the luminaries and declines the torch-race image as an unnecessary change of metaphor, Clarke introduces the fires kept on towers at harbour mouths to guide ships in and carries it into the next clause, Calvin makes us lamps carrying the wick or candlesticks bearing the candle of the doctrine, and Robertson doubts any connection with the preceding figure and thinks the context calls for holding fast

What being blameless amounts to: Gill finds an active sense as well as a passive, that they be without blaming others as well as unblamed, Ellicott distinguishes blamelessness before external law from the inward purity of the second word, and Calvin grants that no such perfection has existed in the world and calls those blameless who aim at it with the whole bent of the mind
outliers: Henry's remark that God's commands were given to be obeyed and not disputed, and that the light of truth and the life of religion are often lost in the heats and mists of disputation

Barnes's reasons why Christians must make the gospel known, that they are kept on earth for the purpose and would otherwise be removed to heaven at once on conversion, and that there is nobody else to do it, since the gay will not warn the gay nor the scoffer the scoffer

Ellicott's tracing of the phrase word of life through its stages, from the disciples' confession that he has the words of eternal life, through his own saying that his words are spirit and life, to the gospel here called a word of life, and at last to the declaration that he himself is the Word of life

Ellicott's picture of Christians as the lesser lights of heaven, dim beside the Sun of Righteousness and seen only in the night of this life, with Robertson's remark that the place for light is the darkness where it is needed
Gill's description of the men who are always finding fault with all persons and things they are concerned with, right or wrong, without any just reason

17.pericope_label: If I be poured out upon the sacrifice of your faith, rejoice with me
debates: What the libation figure is drawn from: Barnes and Clarke both work from the classical drink-offering poured over a victim, Clarke continuing his own metaphor of the mariner who sacrifices on gaining port, while Calvin derives the word instead from the victims by which treaties were confirmed among the ancients, so that the death is the confirmation of their faith, and Robertson declares it uncertain whether heathen or Jewish offerings are meant and the question unimportant

Whose sacrifice is spoken of: Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott take the faith of the Philippians for the sacrifice and the apostle’s blood for the libation poured over it, Ellicott adding that the martyrdom is valued not for itself but as conducing to their own self-sacrifice, apparently contemplated as offered in life rather than in death, while Calvin makes the apostle the priest who had offered them to God by the gospel

Why he asks to learn their state rather than to tell them his: Chrysostom answers that Epaphroditus would have reported his own state before Timothy arrived, Calvin that the expectation of help animates soldiers and would keep them from giving way to impostors, and Ellicott hears in the words some anxiety but greater confidence about the news that would come
outliers: Barnes's story from antiquity of the Athenian who returned from Marathon bleeding and exhausted, rushed into the presence of the magistrates, uttered only the two words rejoice, we rejoice, and immediately expired — the very pair of verbs used here

Ellicott's account of joy in three stages, natural in the first thoughts of childhood, chequered or destroyed by the second thoughts of fuller experience, and returning in the third and deepest thoughts of the Christian, solemnised but deepened into thankfulness

Barnes's argument that the offhand mention of Timothy's earlier presence at Philippi, nowhere stated in the history, is such as would have occurred to no one composing a forgery, and shows the two books to be independent

Robertson's remark that young missionaries offer their lives as a challenge to other Christians to match their money with their blood, and his note that the verb for being of good cheer is common in sepulchral inscriptions
Ellicott's observation that Timothy is spoken of here in the third person, so that although he is joined in the salutation the epistle is the apostle's and his alone
Henry's note that though he was himself a great apostle he took all occasions to speak with respect of those who were far his inferiors

20.pericope_label: I have no man likeminded, for all seek their own
debates: Whom Timothy is said to be like: Robertson insists the adjective means likeminded with Timothy and not with the apostle, so that no one else is his equal, and Calvin reads it the same way as a comparison with the others rather than with Paul, while Gill and Ellicott take it as likeness to the apostle himself

How the saying that all seek their own is to be taken: Wesley alone takes it at full strength and exclaims that only one of all the labourers could be thoroughly approved, while Gill restricts it to the greatest part, Clarke to those who preached of envy and strife, and Calvin denies that they were intent exclusively on their own interests and says only that they were to some extent negligent; Ellicott calls the declaration startling and suggests either accidental separation or a temporary falling away, and Robertson resolves it by observing that Luke must have been away from Rome

How the phrase about the son and the father is construed: Ellicott holds the construction curiously broken, as though the apostle had begun to describe dutiful ministration and then changed in humility to make them fellow-servants, while Clarke and Robertson press the same point from the preposition, that Timothy did not serve the apostle but served with him
outliers: Wesley's phrase for the rarity of such helpers, that few will be found likeminded, willing naked to follow a naked Master

Calvin's complaint that the modesty commended in Timothy has been rare in every age, and that in his own day one would look in vain among the young for anyone who would give way to his seniors in the smallest thing, so far does impertinence prevail
Clarke's remark that apostles and bishops in those times laboured as hard as their deacons, there being no sinecures, every man a labourer and every labourer with his wages

Ellicott's inference from the charge that no man should despise his youth that Timothy's character was gentle and warm-hearted rather than commanding, which is perhaps why so emphatic a commendation was needed
The disagreement over how often the Philippians had seen Timothy, Ellicott counting four occasions from the history and Robertson three
Barnes's plea that the companions should not be judged harshly, since as many professing Christians now would do no better

25.pericope_label: Epaphroditus, my brother and companion in labour and fellow-soldier
debates: Whether the recovery was miraculous, and what follows from it: Clarke and Barnes both report the argument that no miracle is intimated and the event is spoken of as natural, so that the power of working cures visited the apostles only occasionally and did not depend on their own will, and that a forgery would not have spared a miracle here; Ellicott reaches the same conclusion independently, adding that an apostle could not, as our Lord would not, work miracles for his own needs

What the word rendered not regarding his life is: Barnes sets out both readings, the received one meaning not taking pains and the other exposing oneself to danger, and prefers the second as suiting the connection; Clarke names the manuscripts and reports it received into the text; Ellicott renders it having gambled with his life, not merely staked but staked recklessly, and reports though doubts a suggested allusion to the caution money forfeited in a lawsuit; Robertson cites an inscription for the sense

Whether the fourth title marks an office: Ellicott reports and rejects the view, held by interpreters ancient and modern, that the word designates the chief pastor of the Philippian church, on the ground that no example confirms such a use, while Robertson takes it simply as messenger and Wesley refers it to the errand of carrying their contribution
outliers: Calvin's objection to himself, that it is surprising to call a lengthened life a mercy of God when the apostle had shortly before declared that he desired death in preference to life
Robertson's report that the cognate word for riskers was afterwards applied to those Christians who exposed their own lives for the dying and the dead

Ellicott's reading of the phrase less sorrowful, that the recovery would take away the sorrow upon sorrow while the old sorrow of captivity and enforced inactivity remained, so that the profession of perfect joy belongs to the willing spirit and the hint of an unspoken sorrow marks the weakness of the flesh

Calvin's warning that good pastors are precious pearls from God's treasuries, the rarer the more worthy of esteem, that God often punishes ingratitude by depriving us of them, and that there is nothing the instruments of the devil are more intent on than undermining their authority
Calvin's aphorism that sickness is not an excellence, but that it is an excellence not to spare yourself in order to serve Christ

The three independent refusals of identification, Ellicott and Robertson both denying that this man is the Epaphras of another epistle and Gill noting that a freedman of Nero bore the same name at Rome in those years
